Jess Von Bank, co-founder of Now to Next and author of Mother of Disruption, joins Chris Hoyt and Gerry Crispin to talk about what AI is revealing about how we work. In her view, AI didn’t break anything. It exposed rules and systems built for a different era that never served people well to begin with.

Jess walks through the “five wounds of change” that show up in every organization. She explains why fear at work usually points to distrust, and what she means by “system weight,” the friction employees deal with every day. For TA leaders, she gets specific about where AI helps recruiting and where it adds risk. She also covers why recruiters need to validate outcomes, why AI has to be observable, and which parts of hiring should stay a “human-only zone.”

She also argues for replacing the transactional employment contract with something closer to a moral covenant, one where the employer’s job is to help people thrive rather than burn them out. And she explains the maternal lens behind the book, which she says is written for everyone, not just women.

Alan Milburn's report on young people and work came out this week.
Here's why my practice doesn't take on teenagers ... 

At 16 I got a Saturday job cleaning kennels at a vet, answering some phones and making tea. 

Then a fast food job in the kitchen on what we'd now call a zero hours contract: busy weeks meant more shifts, and if you wanted the good ones you worked harder than the person next to you. When the business was quieter and turnover was down.. there were fewer shifts. Nobody felt exploited. It's how I learned what work is, how to be reliable, deal with happy or grumpy clients .

Today kids ask us for a Saturday shift and we say no to every one, because its not worth the hassle.

Yes, the money matters. Since 2020 the minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds has gone from £4.55 to £8.00 an hour, a 76% rise. For 18 to 20-year-olds it's gone from £6.45 to £10.85. Now interestingly .. the CMA launched a full investigation into vets after prices rose around 60% over a similar stretch... but noobody's investigating this.

But the wage isn't the only thing that stops us. It's everything that comes with it. 

Before a 16-year-old touches a mop we need a written contract on day one, right to work checks, a separate young person's risk assessment, and health and safety inductions covering COSHH, manual handling, sharps and fire. In a vet practice there are radiation rules on top. Then data protection training, because they'll be answering the phone. Every one of those needs training, signing, filing and keeping. Add sick pay from day one, and from January an unfair dismissal claim after six months with no cap on the payout. All for five hours every second Saturday.

For years, businesses have told successive governments this was continual rise in wages and NI was stopping us hiring. Now their own review says the same thing. We didn't need a 237 page report, we needed someone to listen.

What would get me saying yes tomorrow:
• A simple first-job contract for under-21s. Kept safe, low wages (its not expected to pay the mortgage or support a family - its a starting salary to teach you about tax, savings, and financial management, hours that flex with the work, and a short term no-fault notice either way - it should be very brief and have a fundamental different legal basis.
• A simple H and S assessment, understanding that we want all our employees to be safe, but understanding that if you make it too much paperwork ... funnily enough, we dont employ people, we move towards tech and AI that can be quickly changed
• Make a Saturday job count, on a record schools and universities recognise.

The best youth employment scheme I ever saw was a Saturday job. 

As businesses, we'd love financial or tax incentives to take young people on, frankly, just get out of the way with the regulations .... 

What's one change that would make you more likely to take on a Saturday morning teenager to work at your business ?

Trust is the real product of an Executive Assistant.
 
An EA sees contracts before they’re signed, HR files, financial records, private calendars, and half-formed decisions. That access is the job. What you do with it is what makes you worth hiring.
 
Why discretion matters:
 
Trust is everything. Founders and executives hand over their inbox, calendar, and documents. Once that trust breaks, no amount of speed makes up for it.
Small leaks cause big damage. A casual remark about a hire, a restructure, or a deal can spread fast and cause real legal, financial, and personal fallout.
Your reputation travels with you. How you talk about past employers tells the next one how you’ll talk about them.
Confidentiality is security. Many breaches start with people: a file sent to the wrong person, an unlocked screen, a shared password.
 
Habits I rely on:
 
Share on a need-to-know basis
Double-check recipients and attachments before sending
Keep shared drive access tight and review it regularly
Use strong, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication, and lock my screen
Keep sensitive talk out of public places and open chats
Never paste confidential material into unapproved apps or public AI tools
Say nothing online about an executive’s schedule, travel, or business
 
Discretion doesn’t end when the job does. When I talk about past work, I talk about skills and results, like managing high email volumes or keeping calendars organized across time zones. Never names, figures, or private details. You can show your value without revealing anything that belongs to someone else.
 
What you should expect from a careful EA: no gossip, asking before assuming something is safe to share, flagging a risk or mistake early, and treating your information the way they’d want theirs treated.
 
Quick and organized is helpful. Quick, organized, and discreet is someone you can rely on completely.
 
If you’re a founder or busy executive looking for support you can trust with the details, let’s talk.
 
What’s the one habit you rely on to keep sensitive information safe? Tell me in the comments.

So the companies building the tools that were meant to replace recruiters are hiring more recruiters than anyone.

My read: the job has changed shape. The recruiters getting hired use AI for the volume work (sourcing lists, screening notes, scheduling, first drafts of outreach) and spend the time they win back on the conversations that close candidates.

Two more things in the data:
→ Only 11% of these roles offer remote working, down from 22% in March.
→ This is mostly a US story. 123 of the roles are in the UK.

The Federal Reserve's October Beige Book has a line on AI and hiring: five of the 12 Districts reported firms that cut staff through attrition, delayed hiring or expected fewer new jobs after investing in AI.

Notice what isn't in that sentence: layoffs. Contacts in the Minneapolis District's IT staffing business said AI wasn't causing layoffs but was dampening the creation of new jobs. In the Atlanta District, most firms didn't expect AI efforts to lead to significant workforce reductions in the near term.

The detail that stayed with me came from the Dallas District. One accounting contact said some large accounting firms are delaying new employment contracts, because they may not need as many entry-level employees as they expected, partly from AI efficiency gains.

Think about where that leads in 5 to 10 years. If software handles the tasks a first-year accountant or engineer would have done, those tasks are where they would have learned what a mistake looks like. In commissioning and validation, the person who executes the test scripts for a few years is usually the one who ends up writing them. Remove that seat and someone has to build the path that replaces it.

Before skipping a junior hire because the software covers the work, a 20-person firm could first list which tasks on that desk teach judgment. Checking a calculation and reading a spec against a submittal are two. Keep a person doing those by hand, with a senior reviewing. The rest can go to the software.

The Beige Book is anecdotes from business contacts, so treat it as a direction.

Interviewer asked me "How can we conduct contract testing using Playwright?" 

First correction I had to do: We cannot conduct contract testing as it natively cannot hold "consumer" & "provider" contracts. But we can explore "json-schema" validations. Which is the next best!

To understand json-schema validation we need 4 steps: 
1) Access to API spec (API Contract)
2) Create Json Schema (generate json schema using: )
3) Store json schema in your framework 
4) Use AJV/ZOD to compile schema and validate with response/request body used/received after execution of API test.

Always remember: JSON Schema validation is one technique used inside contract testing. It is not a synonym for contract testing itself.

What it covers: field presence, data types, required versus optional fields, string formats, nested structure. All of this is expressed once, declaratively, in a schema file.

What it cannot do: 

1) It cannot verify the HTTP status code or response headers were correct.
 
2) It cannot check semantic or business rules a type system cannot express, for example that end_date comes after start_date, or that a total matches the sum of line items.
 
3) It cannot tell you whether the schema reflects a real, agreed contract, or just whatever the API happened to return the one time it was sampled.

Quick tip: If you review the API spec carefully after every change made by Backend teams. Then we can use: "toJsonSchema" to dynamically generate schema using a flag. 
If set to true, it updates the schema files and we just validate the final playwright report.

Building an AI FP&A team | Variance Analysis
 
You voted, and variance analysis won. So here it is.
 
The budget gap is where the conversation starts, not where it ends. “Labor is over budget” doesn’t tell anyone what to do.
 
So the variance agent doesn’t stop at the number.
 
How it works today:
 
• It compares any two versions (say budget vs. latest forecast) by period, account and department, and flags what’s favorable and what’s above the materiality threshold
• For every material labor gap it splits the difference into hiring (more or fewer people than planned), cost per head, and FX
• Other material gaps get a driver tag: FX, CapEx, an assumption change or a contract. FX only when the rate move actually explains the gap
 
A bridge that doesn’t add up is worse than no bridge. So a check makes sure the pieces sum to the variance.
 
And the calculations run in tested code. Claude built it with me and explains the results, but the numbers don’t depend on a chat.
 
A few things have also been added since my previous post: a full cash statement (loans, interest, tax and VAT), a P&L in standard EBITDA-to-net-income order, and more reconciliation checks on the Data Health tab.
 
And the next step is already underway. I'm now working with a company to connect the system to their real data. It's only the beginning, but the connection was quick and stable, and the system already shows their numbers. The reconciliation checks have also surfaced first findings, including differences inside the source data itself.
 
My main takeaway: the value of variance analysis is the sentence after the number. Here, full-year labor cost is $559K over budget, but not because of hiring: we have fewer people than planned (−$82K), and FX adds an estimated $593K. That’s a very different conversation.
 
(Screenshots: demo company, fictional numbers.)
 
When you review a variance, how much of the gap do you usually manage to explain, and who owns the rest?
 
P.S. Next up: cash & runway or the what-if simulator?

A new name for a projectI have been building: #Allocwise is now #915am — Allocation Planner.

The name is inspired by the 9:15 AM market open, reflected in a clock symbol fixed at 9:15 in the app’s branding.

The idea behind the project remains simple:
How can I see where a portfolio stands today—and what changes when I add fresh money?

915am turns a spreadsheet-style allocation workflow into an interactive web app. The current prototype lets you:
 - Compare current allocations with target weights
 - Explore planned additions across holdings
 - Split fresh money in proportion to allocation shortfalls
 - Flag holdings above a configurable single-stock threshold
 - Export a plan to CSV

Built with React, TypeScript, Zustand, Recharts, and Tailwind CSS, with portfolio entries saved in the current browser.

One useful lesson from the build: a chart can look right while telling the wrong story. During review, I found that the “target” bars were displaying post-addition allocations rather than the actual targets. Correcting that reinforced the importance of checking what a visualization represents—not just how it looks.

I used AI-assisted iteration to refine the interface, troubleshoot issues, and review changes. This is still a working prototype, with mobile usability improvements and further validation in progress.

This project reflects what I enjoy about reporting and automation: turning numbers and rules into something clearer and easier to use.

The design job market right now: fewer openings, more competition, and a stronger case for good design
 
Let’s be honest: landing a design job is harder today than it was a couple of years ago. Not because design matters less, but because of the economy.
 
What’s happening:
 → When money is expensive and investors are cautious, companies put new products on hold, and the hiring that comes with them.
 → Every headcount gets scrutinized, and design often lands in the “can wait” pile.
 → AI tools have sped up the routine work, so one designer is now expected to cover more: research, UI, prototyping, metrics.
 → Each opening draws hundreds of applications, many from strong people affected by layoffs.
 
Why I’m still optimistic:
 When budgets get tight, the products that win are the ones that are easier and clearer to use than the competition. Good design isn’t a cost center. It’s conversion, retention, and fewer support tickets. Companies that keep investing in UX through a downturn come out of it stronger. Markets move in cycles, and those teams are the first to start hiring again.

I’ve just seen my first casualty of the workers’ rights reform.

A candidate of mine interviewed for a permanent, full-time role and got the offer! Great news...but it came through as a 6-month fixed-term contract instead.

Six months is no accident. From 1 January, people get unfair dismissal rights after six months instead of two years, and compensation will be uncapped.

Look at what job seekers are up against right now:

-Higher employer NI making every hire cost more
-Automation and AI investment replacing roles before they’re even advertised
-Cost of living squeezing the whole economy
-Unprecedented times: mass tech layoffs and both ends of the job market being squeezed

And now some hiring teams are nervous to commit in case it goes wrong. The bigger the job, the longer it can take to show impact, and 6 months is cutting it fine. SMEs don’t necessarily have the luxury of an in-house HR team to hold their hand. Employers are stuck between a rock and a hard place.

I understand that workers need protections, but these rights were meant to give people more security, and FTCs can be the total opposite of job security.

Is anyone else seeing this happen?

There’s a strange disconnect when you’ve spent more than twenty-five years building and running technology for serious organisations, and you still can’t get past the first screen of an application. I applied for a role this week and had an automated rejection back in under 24 hours, saying my application was unlikely to progress.

I’ve been an IT and transformation leader since before most of today’s tooling existed. I built an IT function from nothing at General Dynamics UK, working with military personnel at MOD Abbey Wood and through MOD budget cycles. Since then I’ve led delivery and governance at HID Global/ASSA ABLOY, IGT, ghd, EDF Renewables, VetPartners and Armstrong Watson. Yet here I am, being filtered out before a human has read a word. I’m not too proud to step sideways, take a contract or move industries. But I do wonder whether recruitment now leans so heavily on AI and keyword matching that it overlooks real experience, judgement and what a person actually delivers. I know I’m not the only one, and that doesn’t make it less disheartening. 

All I want to know is WHO is getting these interviews, if someone like me isn’t, and so many people I know aren’t either?

So, to turn a frustrating job search into something useful, here’s a reminder of what I bring. I’ve run Agile delivery and ITIL governance throughout my career. I’ve led Azure and Microsoft 365 migrations, and a Microsoft Fabric and Azure data platform build. I’ve moved the full Sage accounting suite and HubSpot CRM into Dynamics 365. I’ve worked across defence, renewable energy, gaming, security technology, veterinary care and professional services. I work for the COO or CFO and alongside the CTO, turning messy technology estates into things the business can run, trust and explain to a board.

I’m also hands-on with AI. I use large language models every day, both to build working software and to get real work done. This year I’ve built and shipped a stack of applications, some with AI assistants built in. I also teach others how to use these tools well: where they help, where they get things wrong, and how to use them safely and with proper governance. I’d rather show you than describe it.

So if you’d rather talk to an actual human with decades of delivery behind them than sift through another few hundred AI-polished applications, hi, I’m Richard. I’m a real person, and I can sort out your technology better than another dashboard can. 🤝

A difficult UK economy can give businesses a reason to change their leadership, not just freeze recruitment.

There are reports of renewed momentum in UK executive hiring despite economic challenges. That does not prove the economy is causing an increase, but it raises an important distinction: recruiting more leaders and recruiting a different kind of leader are not the same thing.

For CEO, MD and COO appointments, we have noticed a "human" centred shift in the brief recently to combine strong commercial acumen with a genuinely human-centred approach.

That means someone who understands margins, cash flow and growth, but also spends time with employees, listens to clients and customers, and acts on what they hear.

Those are not competing priorities. A customer conversation can expose a service problem before it becomes a lost contract. Customers, Clients and Employees are looking to Executive Leadership to inspire, engage, trust and lead. Listening to and hearing what employees and customers/clients are saying can reveal that 1% of difference that delivers longer term commercial value and success.

With the speed and advancement of technology and tech innovation/AI, we are starting to realise what skills/behaviours are important and it always comes back to human connection with tech enabled efficiency. 

From a Search perspective, the assessment needs to test both sides. Alongside the standard sales/commercial and revenue we need to think deeper and get "under the bonnet" of the people we meet.

At Disrupt we refer to "People Architecture" and see this as a key component of any Search or recruitment process.  

Emotional intelligence and the ability to adapt to your environment is now a non-negotiable to long term survival. Without this how can we win the hearts and minds of the people to put in the hard work so we can all thrive? 

So how are Boards, Co-founders and Executive leadership assessing this?

Are you going beyond the standard questions at interview stage or just recycling the process created in the 1980's?

Truly understanding the people that you are trusting to lead your business should not be underestimated; ask candidates for evidence of how they handled difficult decisions, retained trust, transformed engagement, and test how they received feedback and altered their course for success. 

The strongest appointment should not require a choice between commercial discipline or human engagement. The brief should demand evidence of both.

5 Critical Compliance Mistakes Companies Must Avoid in Hiring 💡

Are you confident your hiring practices are fully compliant worldwide? 💼 Compliance mistakes in recruitment can cost you big — fines, legal battles, and damaged reputation.

Here are 5 critical compliance pitfalls companies must avoid:

✅ Worker Misclassification: Mislabeling employees as contractors can lead to hefty penalties and unpaid benefits claims. Always assess local laws and consider an Employer of Record (EOR) for international hires.

✅ AI Hiring Regulations: AI tools speed up hiring but come with strict rules on transparency, bias audits, and candidate consent. Regularly audit your AI systems to stay legally safe.

✅ Localize Employment Contracts: Don’t use one-size-fits-all contracts. Adapt to local labor laws—covering wages, benefits, and termination—to avoid disputes and fines.

✅ Data Privacy: Handling candidate data incorrectly can result in severe penalties. Ensure explicit consent, secure data transfers, and compliance with GDPR, CCPA, and other laws.

✅ Pay Transparency & Equity: New laws require clear salary ranges and gender pay gap reporting. Being transparent boosts trust and attracts top talent.

A difficult UK economy can give businesses a reason to change their leadership, not just freeze recruitment.

There are reports of renewed momentum in UK executive hiring despite economic challenges. That does not prove the economy is causing an increase, but it raises an important distinction: recruiting more leaders and recruiting a different kind of leader are not the same thing.

For CEO, MD and COO appointments, we have noticed a "human" centred shift in the brief recently to combine strong commercial acumen with a genuinely human-centred approach.

That means someone who understands margins, cash flow and growth, but also spends time with employees, listens to clients and customers, and acts on what they hear.

Those are not competing priorities. A customer conversation can expose a service problem before it becomes a lost contract. Customers, Clients and Employees are looking to Executive Leadership to inspire, engage, trust and lead. Listening to and hearing what employees and customers/clients are saying can reveal that 1% of difference that can make the difference to longer term commercial value.

With the speed and advancement of technology and tech innovation/AI, we are starting to realise what skills/behaviours are important and it always comes back to human connection with tech enabled efficiency. 

From a Search perspective, the assessment needs to test both sides. Alongside the standard sales/commercial and revenue we need to think deeper and get "under the bonnet" of the people we meet.

At Disrupt we refer to "People Architecture" and see this as a key component of any Search or recruitment process.  

Emotional intelligence and the ability to adapt to your environment is now a non-negotiable to long term survival. Without this how can we win the hearts and minds of the people to put in the hard work so we can all thrive? 

So how are Boards, Co-founders and Executive leadership assessing this?

Are you going beyond the standard questions at interview stage or just recycling the process created in the 1980's?

Truly understanding the people that you are trusting to lead your business should noit be underestimated; ask candidates for evidence of how they handled difficult decisions, retained trust, transformed engagement, and test how they received feedback and altered their course for success? 

The strongest appointment should not require a choice between commercial discipline or human engagement. The brief should demand evidence of both.

Everyone wants to talk about what AI can do with their numbers. Far fewer people are asking whether the numbers are right in the first place.

You can have a dashboard that looks brilliant and tells you something that isn't true. Lovely charts but a profit figure that's out by tens of thousands because half the month hasn't been reconciled properly. 

AI doesn't fix that. It just gets you to the wrong answer faster, and explains it more confidently than any of us would.

Which is why I think bookkeeping matters more now than it ever has. 

For years it's been treated as the bit of the finance function to get done as cheaply as possible, the admin that sits underneath the interesting stuff. I'd argue it's the other way round. 

It's the foundation, and everything you do with your numbers is only ever as good as what's underneath it.

When you know you can rely on your numbers at any point, a lot changes:

👥 Hiring: you know what the business can carry, and for how long, before anyone signs a contract.

💷 Paying yourself: you take what the business can genuinely afford, at the right time and in the most tax efficient way, without leaving a surprise for year end.

🏷️ Pricing: you can see the real gross margin on each product, service or customer, and change prices because the numbers say so rather than because it feels about right.

📅 Tax bills: VAT, corporation tax and the quiet months show up on the forecast long before they hit the bank.

🏦 Banks and buyers: when someone asks for figures, you can send them the same day and they stand up to questions.

🤖 AI: the tools everyone is excited about become genuinely useful, because what you're feeding them is right.

None of that works on numbers you have to second guess. 

Getting the bookkeeping right isn't glamorous, and done properly it's never going to be the cheapest option. 

But it's the difference between numbers that tell you what happened and numbers you can actually make decisions with.

You can't make a good decision on a bad number, however nice the chart looks.

Software engineering roadmaps can be fully approved and still be under-resourced.
A business can have funding, stakeholder buy-in and a clear product or technology strategy.

But there’s another question worth asking:

Do we actually have the engineering capability to deliver it?
That becomes especially important when delivery depends on specialist expertise across software engineering, solution architecture, cloud, DevOps, QA automation, data engineering and AI.

I think workforce planning needs to happen alongside delivery planning, not six months later when critical milestones are at risk because key skills aren't available.

Before committing to the next phase, I'd be asking:
→ Do we have the right engineering capability in-house?
→ Where are we overly dependent on key individuals?
→ Which skills are readily available in the market, and which are becoming increasingly difficult to secure?
→ Where does permanent hiring make sense versus contract resource?
→ What capabilities will we need 12-24 months from now that we don't have today?

Software delivery isn't only about roadmaps, budgets and technology choices.
It's about having the right people with the right expertise available at the right time.
The organisations delivering successfully aren't just planning products and platforms. They're planning capability.

If you're reviewing your software engineering strategy for 2027, I'd be happy to share what I'm seeing across the market regarding skill availability, hiring trends and where the most significant talent shortages are emerging.

Six months ago, a tech founder and old friend called me in a panic. Let’s call him Vikram.
For 14 years, he lived the classic Indian IT dream—250 engineers across Pune and Hyderabad, steady US clients, and 22% EBITDA margins built on one simple formula:
More problems = More billable hours = More hiring.

Then came the renewal call with his largest US healthcare client (25% of his revenue). Vikram pitched a 50-engineer team for an 18-month legacy modernization project.
The CTO paused and said:"Our 6 internal engineers used AI agents to migrate two modules over the weekend. Tell me how you deliver this in 4 months with 8 people—or we’re taking it in-house."

Dead silence.

Across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, and Gurugram, the $250B+ Indian IT services playbook is breaking. For 30 years, we won on labor arbitrage. You cannot beat an AI agent costing pennies by throwing cheaper freshers at the problem.

The signs are everywhere: → Top IT firms have decoupled revenue from headcount, shedding 60,000+ net roles while growing top line. → US procurement teams now bake a mandatory 25–40% "AI productivity discount" into renewal RFPs. → The billing pyramid is dead. Clients refuse to pay to train your juniors when AI agents outperform 1-year coders in QA and support.

Wait for the storm to pass, and your bench will bleed you dry.
Here is the exact 3-step pivot Vikram and I mapped out—and what he executed over the last 6 months:
1. Cannibalize your own billing first Before a rival undercuts you, walk into your client’s room and cut your own quote by 20% using internal AI workflows. Your top line dips, but your gross margin jumps from 22% to 45%—and you lock out every competitor.
2. Sell outcomes + IP, not naked resumes Stop pitching "10 QA engineers." Sell an Automated AI Testing Engine run by 2 Senior Architects. Package your own migration scripts and agents, and charge for milestones—not timesheets.
3. Follow the enterprise data mess 85% of US enterprises can't deploy AI because their data is trapped in legacy silos. Move your bench out of shrinking web-dev contracts and into Data Engineering, AI Governance, and Agentic Workflows.

Last Tuesday, I caught up with Vikram again. Six months after that call:
Headcount: Down 15%
Revenue: Flat
Net Profit: Up 38%
And that US CTO just signed a 2-year expansion—because Vikram stopped acting like a staffing vendor and became an engineering partner.
Indian IT survived Y2K, 2008, and Cloud. We will survive this too—but only if we burn the old playbook today.

Founders & delivery heads: are your US/UK clients already demanding "AI discounts" on renewals?

A hiring manager's most expensive hour is the interview that should never have happened.

So we do the filtering before you see a name. Every engineer we put forward passes four layers:

1. Profile and right to work. The CV can be checked and the person can legally take the contract.
2. Communication screen. Can they explain a decision? Do they say "I don't know" when it is true?
3. Written technical assessment. They reason about code they did not write, which is what joining your team really looks like.
4. Live technical interview. With an engineer, in your stack, against written criteria.

You then receive a short list with a written scorecard for each person, including our reservations. A shortlist with no weaknesses listed is a sales document, and you have read enough of those.

Typically: shortlist in 5 to 10 days, engineer started 1 to 4 weeks from the brief.
